node.label: Michel-Rolph Trouillot
node.date_label: Ti dife boule sou istwa Ayiti 1977 · Peasants and Capital 1988 · Haiti: State against Nation 1990 · 'The Odd and the Ordinary' 1990 · Silencing the Past 1995 · Global Transformations 2003 · Trouillot Remixed 2021
node.description: A Haitian anthropologist and historian who left Port-au-Prince for New York in 1968 and wrote his first history of the Haitian Revolution in Creole (Ti dife boule, 1977). Peasants and Capital (1988) and Haiti: State against Nation (1990) studied Dominica's economy and Duvalierism; 'The Odd and the Ordinary' (1990) refused Haitian exceptionalism. Silencing the Past (1995) asked how power enters 'the production of history': silences enter at four moments, 'fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance'; 'in history, power begins at the source' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020); the Haitian Revolution was 'unthinkable' as it happened, and the 'historical guild' relegated 'racism, slavery and colonialism' to 'an historical backburner' (p. 98, as quoted by Craipain). 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot' and Global Transformations (2003) turned the same question on anthropology's 'North Atlantic universals'. Craipain: Silencing the Past 'remains an unavoidable reference' (2024); Daut asked readers to go 'beyond Trouillot' (2021). Trouillot Remixed (2021) collects the essays.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Michel-Rolph Trouillot (1949–2012); Ti dife boule sou istwa Ayiti (1977; Stirring the Pot of Haitian History, 2021); Peasants and Capital: Dominica in the World Economy (1988); Haiti: State against Nation: The Origins and Legacy of Duvalierism (1990); 'The Odd and the Ordinary: Haiti, the Caribbean, and the World' (Cimarrón, 1990); Silencing the Past: Power and the Production of History (1995; 20th-anniversary edition 2015, foreword Hazel V. Carby); Open the Social Sciences (Gulbenkian Commission, 1996); 'Abortive Rituals: Historical Apologies in the Global Era' (2000); 'Culture on the Edges' (2002); Global Transformations: Anthropology and the Modern World (2003), including 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot' (first printing reported as 1991, not verified) and 'The Anthropology of the State in the Age of Globalization'; Trouillot Remixed (2021). Readers: Alyssa Goldstein Sepinwall (2013); Colin Dayan, J. Michael Dash, Greg Beckett (2013); Hazel V. Carby (2015); Rodrigo Bulamah, Júlia Goyatá and Bethânia Pereira (2020); Marlene L. Daut (2021); Yarimar Bonilla (2021); Bastien Craipain (2024).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-archive.md §§4, 13): the University of Chicago obituary (2012) and the Chicago Library finding aid's biographical note (in full); the contents and descriptions of Silencing the Past (Beacon), Global Transformations (Springer, with the 'Savage Slot' abstract) and Trouillot Remixed (Duke); the Journal of Haitian Studies 19:2 (2013) contents; Craipain's H-Net review of Stirring the Pot (2024, in full); the Bulamah–Goyatá–Pereira introduction to 'The Odd and the Ordinary' (Vibrant, 2020, in part); Davidson's Overland essay (2020), which quotes chapter 1 without page numbers. Unread: every book's body — the four-moments passage of Silencing the Past is given as later writers list it and as Davidson quotes it, unpaginated, and its wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1; chapter 3, 'An Unthinkable History', by title and Craipain's quotation (p. 98) only; Haiti: State against Nation and Peasants and Capital by obituary citations only; Sepinwall (2013), Daut (2021), Carby (2015), Bonilla's prelude (2021) and Dayan (2012–13) are named as readers but unread. The first printing of 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot' (reported as 1991), the Current Anthropology date of the state essay (reported as 2001) and the dates of the Johns Hopkins chair and Institute are not verified by a page read and are not asserted. Wikidata Q6836249 checked by QLever on 2026-10-23. Born 26 November 1949, Port-au-Prince (Wikidata); son and nephew of the historians Ernest and Hénock Trouillot (Bulamah et al., n. 3); Duke 1983–88, Johns Hopkins 1988–98, Chicago 1998–2012 (finding aid); died 5 July 2012 aged 62 after an aneurysm (obituaries). History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23): cited by 5.9% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25 (0.8% in 2000–09), Silencing the Past by 4.3% in 2015–25, in 5 of 18 fields; a figure for this note, not for arrows.

incident_edges.relationship: Silencing the Past (1995) placed the archive inside the production of history: silences enter at 'the moment of fact creation (the making of sources)', 'fact assembly (the making of archives)', 'fact retrieval (the making of narratives)' and 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)'; 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' (all as quoted by Davidson, 2020); Stoler's 2002 essay cites it three times
incident_edges.evidence_note: Davidson 2020 (read, unpaginated), which reproduces the four-moments passage as a block quotation ('Silences enter the process of historical production at four crucial moments: the moment of fact creation (the making of sources); the moment of fact assembly (the making of archives); the moment of fact retrieval (the making of narratives); and the moment of retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)') and quotes 'in history, power begins at the source' and 'archives are the institutions that organise facts and sources' as Trouillot's words; Beacon contents; Stoler 2002 nn. 24, 38, 49 (reference list read). Body unread; corrected after review (finding 13). Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).
incident_edges.map_label: Silences and the making of archives, 1995

incident_edges.relationship: The Haitian Revolution as 'An Unthinkable History' (1995, ch. 3): the 'historical guild' facilitated 'the relegation to an historical backburner of the three themes to which [the Haitian Revolution] was linked: racism, slavery and colonialism' (p. 98, as quoted by Craipain); Ti dife boule (1977) told the revolution in Creole; Haiti: State against Nation (1990) its Duvalierist legacy
incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full), quoting p. 98 and dating Ti dife boule to the Brooklyn Koléksion Lakansièl, 1977; the Chicago obituary and finding aid for the 1977 and 1990 books; Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira on the 1990 book as 'the classic' (para. 2, read). Chapter 3 unread.

incident_edges.relationship: 'Anthropology and the Savage Slot: The Poetics and Politics of Otherness' (Global Transformations, 2003) and the book as a whole: 'Anthropology discovered globalization before the term became fashionable' (chapter abstract); the discipline's concepts of culture, modernity and globalization as 'North Atlantic universals' (as read by Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira, 2020); 'Adieu, Culture: A New Duty Arises'
incident_edges.evidence_note: Springer abstract of ch. 2 (read); Springer contents; Bulamah et al. 2020, para. 5 (read); Duke contents of Trouillot Remixed for the essay's place. The 'savage slot' thesis itself was not read; the label uses the title.
incident_edges.map_label: The savage slot and North Atlantic universals, 2003

incident_edges.relationship: Global Transformations (2003): 'North Atlantic Fictions: Global Transformations, 1492–1945', 'A Fragmented Globality' and 'The Anthropology of the State in the Age of Globalization' set the North Atlantic's production of 'the West' against the anthropology of globalization (Springer description); Peasants and Capital (1988) placed Dominica 'in the World Economy'
incident_edges.evidence_note: Springer book page (description and contents, read); the Chicago obituary for the 1988 book. Bodies unread.
incident_edges.map_label: The West as a North Atlantic fiction, 1988–2003

incident_edges.relationship: Ti dife boule sou istwa Ayiti (Brooklyn, 1977), a Creole history of the revolution written in exile by a group that 'harbored an anti- or rather a counter-academism … to oppose the knowledge embargo imposed by the "official" venues of knowledge production' (Lyonel Trouillot, as quoted by Craipain); 'virtually absent from bibliographies in North Atlantic academia' until the 2021 translation
incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full), quoting the Liverpool edition's preface (p. xxiii) and Jonassaint's afterword (p. 182); the Chicago obituary; the finding aid ('fleeing the Duvalier regime', 1968).
incident_edges.map_label: A Creole history against the guild, 1977–2021

incident_edges.relationship: Silencing the Past 'remains an unavoidable reference for anyone navigating the streams of Black and Caribbean studies in academia and beyond' (Craipain, 2024); Bulamah, Goyatá and Pereira read 'The Odd and the Ordinary' as challenging an exceptionalist image that isolates Haiti from its surrounding world (2020, paragraph 5)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full); Bulamah et al. 2020, paras 3–5 (read). Corrected after review (finding 7): the phrase 'dominated by Christianity, capitalism, and whiteness' (1990a: 7) describes the surrounding world, not Haiti's exceptionalist image, and is no longer quoted here.
incident_edges.map_label: Haiti in Black and Caribbean studies, 1990–2024

incident_edges.relationship: 'A critical indictment of Western historiography and its systematic disregard for Haiti's contribution to emancipatory struggles and decolonial politics', offering 'an eye-opening analysis of the epistemological failures and ideological maneuverings intrinsic to history telling as a professional activity' (Craipain, 2024); 'As Trouillot taught us, not all narratives or narrators are created equal'
incident_edges.evidence_note: Craipain 2024 (read in full). Trouillot's own words for this claim are only Davidson's unpaginated quotations ('Power is constitutive of the story'). Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).

incident_edges.relationship: 'The Presence in the Past' (1995, ch. 5), 'Good Day, Columbus: Silences, Power, and Public History (1492–1892)' and 'Abortive Rituals: Historical Apologies in the Global Era' (2000) took commemoration and apology as moments of 'retrospective significance (the making of history in the final instance)' (as quoted by Davidson, 2020); in Davidson's exposition, silences are produced and reproduced throughout any telling of a story
incident_edges.evidence_note: Chapter and essay titles (Beacon and Duke contents, read); Davidson 2020 (read), whose block quotation gives the fourth moment in Trouillot's words; the sentence 'Silences are produced and reproduced throughout any telling of a story' is Davidson's own exposition, not a Trouillot quotation (corrected after review, finding 13). Thin: no body read. Wording awaits re-verification on a library copy of Silencing the Past, ch. 1 (precedent: the Chandavarkar 1997 quotations in 1.152).

incident_edges.relationship: O’Brien uses Trouillot’s account of unequal historical production and archival power to analyze local histories and public commemoration.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own selected public indexedxvii/xxiand56explicitly name Trouillot when widening historical production beyond professional historians, treating local histories as an archive, and considering public meanings made through commemoration. A particular theoretical resource, not sole genealogy or a claim that the full primary pages were read.
